section_summary: This section examines proposed British and American economic pressure on Japan, Japan’s production plans, and the effects of wartime controls on American businesses. A long consular report surveys banking, shipping, petroleum, automobiles, films, cotton, dyes, and lumber. Later items address Japan’s trade and currency strains, monthly economic conditions, and reported shortages and public dissatisfaction.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of article on economic pressure and a New East Asia
subfiles.about: A concluding argument urges Japan to withstand possible Anglo-American economic pressure.
subfiles.summary: Calls for national endurance while Japan establishes a “New East Asia.”

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on sanctions discussion
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Grew’s objections to the British Ambassador’s case for sanctions against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew doubts that sanctions would yield a face-saving Japanese retreat. He stresses differences between British and American interests in China and Japan’s continued capacity to fight.

subfiles.title: Addition to sanctions discussion
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew comments on Craigie’s proposal for joint economic measures against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew distinguishes American from British interests in East Asia and questions the risks and likely effectiveness of sanctions. He argues that Japan would not accept merely nominal gains in China and that its different approaches to Britain and the United States reflect different conflicts of interest.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Craigie’s telegram to the British Foreign Office
subfiles.about: Craigie advocates prompt British and American economic countermeasures against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Craigie proposes reducing purchases of Japanese goods and gold and restricting Japan’s access to raw materials and shipping facilities. He judges the risk of war slight if measures are handled discreetly and Japanese officials can save face.

subfiles.title: Japan: Plan for expansion of production
subfiles.from: R. B. Pape, Assistant Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes a three-year Japanese plan to expand production of strategic goods.
subfiles.summary: Lists proposed increases in metals, fuel, chemicals, machinery, vehicles, and other products across Japan, Manchukuo, and North China. The report estimates a large investment and cautions that the plan’s feasibility remains unproven.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for despatch no. 3987
subfiles.about: Directs the reader to an original despatch filed under another number.

subfiles.title: Problems confronting some American firms in Japan
subfiles.from: George A. Makinson, American Consul General, Osaka
subfiles.about: Surveys the effects of Japanese wartime economic controls on American businesses.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the decline of foreign banking and trans-Pacific shipping business, petroleum quotas, automobile assembly restrictions, and curbs on films and Kodak products. It examines shrinking American cotton, dye, and lumber trade under import and exchange controls. Makinson expects state-directed industry, lower living standards, and development in Japan’s controlled areas to reduce future American commercial opportunities.

subfiles.title: Economic phase in the Far East
subfiles.doc_type: press clipping reproduced in military attaché report
subfiles.from: The Times Tokyo correspondent; forwarded by William Wayer, Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s shrinking exports, gold reserves, currency struggle, and wartime price pressures.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that Japan’s trade deficit and declining gold reserves constrain its plans for a yen bloc in China. It discusses inflation, labor, savings, and state control, concluding that economic danger is growing but is not immediate.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on July 1939 economic conditions
subfiles.about: Points to the original report on Japan’s July economic and financial conditions.
subfiles.summary: References despatch no. 4108 in file 894.00 P.R./140.

subfiles.title: General economic and financial conditions
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo, with the Commercial Attaché’s office
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese business, prices, crops, markets, rice distribution, and industrial mergers in July.
subfiles.summary: Notes rising silk and food prices, a stronger stock market, steady foreign exchange, a new Japan Rice Company, and mergers among heavy-industry firms. The excerpt ends mid-sentence.

subfiles.title: Request for report on Japanese consumer restrictions
subfiles.doc_type: Department of State instruction with routing pages
subfiles.about: Requests a detailed report on restrictions, living conditions, and public reactions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cites press accounts of fiber goods, food rationing, labor shortages, and juvenile labor, and asks the Embassy to investigate with consular assistance.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting report on Japanese consumer restrictions
subfiles.about: Requests an Embassy report on reported shortages and dissatisfaction among Japanese consumers.
subfiles.summary: Repeats press claims about fiber goods, leather, food, farm labor, and juvenile labor, and asks for a comprehensive mailed report.

subfiles.title: Japanese Begin to Complain
subfiles.from: Mark J. Ginsbourg, The Washington Post
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese complaints about shortages and wartime labor demands.
subfiles.summary: Reports scarce cotton, leather and food, labor shortages, long workdays, and rising prices.
